intro: A broad string melody and a lighter dance share the third movement of Rimsky-Korsakov’s suite. How does the return of the longer line change after the quicker music?
question: How does a long melody make room for a dance?

relations.label: The broad song returns
relations.basis: The lyrical A material returns after the lighter dance in the movement’s outer-section design. This brief sustained match agrees with the return marked near 260 s, without identifying a precise violin entrance. CENS diagonal mean 0.938, sustained 12.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 261 s (cache/form/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-prince.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A melody in long breaths
cues.text: The broad opening melody combines sustained notes with small turns and ornaments. Follow the long line through its decoration, noticing how the slower accompaniment supports it without copying every movement.
cues.evidence: This describes the score’s opening string melody and accompaniment, not an instrument entrance detected from the audio.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A composer in the navy
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov trained as a naval officer and spent three years at sea. He began his First Symphony before that voyage and later worked as an inspector of naval bands, alongside his composing and teaching.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note records the naval training, voyage, symphony and band-inspection work.

cues.title: Under the long line
cues.text: During the extended opening span, listen below the melody. Changes in the bass can redirect the harmony while the upper line keeps its singing shape; the two parts need not move at the same rate.
cues.evidence: This is a listening guide to melody and accompaniment across the opening section, without a second-specific harmonic claim.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Breathing between phrases
cues.text: The long melody contains withdrawals as well as swells. Follow the shape across several phrases, noticing how a reduction in weight can separate them without a sharp accent or complete silence.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls around 1:45–1:50 and rises again towards 1:55, supporting the broader rise-and-fall pattern.

cues.title: Between song and dance
cues.text: The opening song and the lighter dance differ in the size and spacing of their gestures. Across the transition, listen for shorter figures gaining prominence while the broader phrase recedes.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the contrasting materials; lower relative level and more frequent attacks around 2:35–2:50 support the approximate transition.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Titles, not a screenplay
cues.text: The suite draws on The Thousand and One Nights. In his autobiography Rimsky-Korsakov called the movement titles hints for listeners, not a detailed programme assigning each musical phrase to a plot incident.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass’s LA Phil note quotes this explanation from Rimsky-Korsakov’s My Musical Life.

cues.title: Colour and weight can differ
cues.text: Within the dance, compare the upper edge of the sound with the strength of the whole phrase. A lighter response can retain a bright colour; brightness and loudness are not interchangeable descriptions.
cues.evidence: Upper-frequency energy remains high around 3:35 even though relative level falls substantially.

cues.title: Towards the opening song
cues.text: The broad lyrical material returns after the quicker dance. Compare its longer phrases with the opening, allowing for the different accompaniment and surrounding activity rather than expecting a literal replay.
cues.evidence: The score’s return is placed approximately; the report finds fewer attacks around 4:20–4:25 but cannot identify a returning melody by itself.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Professor at twenty-seven
cues.text: In 1871 Rimsky-Korsakov accepted a professorship at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory. His autobiography describes himself at that point as still an amateur: the appointment preceded the mature reputation for orchestral craft associated with this suite.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s LA Phil biography gives the appointment and reports the composer’s retrospective description of his training.

cues.title: A more exposed line
cues.text: The reduced middle span offers a contrast to the weight of the full ensemble. Keep the suite’s recurring solo-violin storytelling role in mind while comparing freer, exposed phrasing with the larger orchestral statements.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the solo role; low relative levels across roughly 5:00–5:30 support a reduced passage, not a timed violin identification.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Weight without faster notes
cues.text: As the lyrical span builds again, distinguish increased weight from increased speed. A long note can ride over a growing accompaniment without the melody itself becoming more rapid.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises across 5:45–6:05 while detected attacks become less frequent.

cues.title: San Francisco, March 1942
cues.text: The recording source identifies Pierre Monteux, the San Francisco Symphony and solo violinist Naoum Blinder. It gives sessions on 3–4 March 1942 at the War Memorial Opera House and describes a transfer from Victor’s 78-rpm set DM-920.
cues.evidence: The Commons file description gives these personnel, session details and disc-set identification.

cues.title: The final large expansion
cues.text: The late span contrasts a quiet preparation with another large expansion. Follow the long phrase across that change of scale, rather than counting only its strongest attacks.
cues.evidence: The strongest detected change is near 6:50, followed by one of the recording’s highest relative-level windows around 7:05.

cues.title: Weight falling away
cues.text: The closing span withdraws from the earlier full sound. Compare the scale of its phrases with the final expansion, attending to what remains distinct as the overall level recedes.
cues.evidence: Relative level and upper-frequency energy both fall across 7:25–7:40.

cues.title: A quiet close within the suite
cues.text: This movement ends quietly, but the suite has another movement to come. Its later festival and shipwreck belong to a different part of the work; this closing passage completes the lyrical scene.
cues.evidence: The suite’s movement order supplies the context; the recording’s relative level falls steeply in its final seconds.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The long line acquires a dancing surface
transitions.how: The broad string song has already moved beyond its opening G major before the lighter Allegretto takes over. Rimsky-Korsakov shortens the gestures, lightens the bass accompaniment and gives the wind figures a more detached profile; the snare-drum rhythm adds a different kind of attack. The dance is related to the lyrical material rather than an unrelated inserted number. Listen for the long melodic contour being reorganised into smaller, more regularly articulated units.
transitions.evidence: The B boundary is 2:35; relative level falls while detected attacks rise from 0.8 per second at 2:25 to 4.6 at 2:40. The score supplies the Allegretto and percussion-led articulation. Paul Serotsky describes the dance as a variation of related material at http://musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm; no precise modulation is inferred from the audio keys.

transitions.title: A broad orchestral gesture restores the song
transitions.how: The dance expands into a broader, trumpet-led gesture, then the original pace and G-major song regain the foreground. D-major dominant harmony directs the bass towards G, while longer melodic values replace the dance’s closely articulated figures. The return changes both scale and function: the orchestra no longer marks out a light dance but supports the sustained string line. Familiar melody supplies the link across the change of gait.
transitions.evidence: The A′ boundary is approximately 4:20, where detected attacks become less frequent. The relations file matches 5.5–18 s with 266.5–279 s, supporting the returning song. The score supplies the dominant-to-G-major route and tempo restoration; Serotsky describes the trumpet-led transition at http://musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm.

transitions.title: The string section yields to one violin
transitions.how: The renewed song thins until a solo violin can take over the melodic foreground. Its ornamented, freer line recalls the suite’s recurring storyteller music rather than merely reducing the string melody to one player. Harp-supported space replaces the ensemble’s continuous weight, and the bass no longer stamps each phrase as firmly. The join connects this movement with the larger suite through instrumental identity and remembered contour, not through a newly announced dance tune.
transitions.evidence: The Reduced texture boundary is 5:00; relative level falls across 4:45–5:00 and stays low through much of 5:30. The score supplies the solo-violin recollection and harp-supported writing. The report anchors the reduction, not the violin’s precise entry, a particular bass note or a new key.

transitions.title: The individual line rejoins the orchestral song
transitions.how: The exposed solo episode gives way to a renewed G-major orchestral statement. Rimsky-Korsakov restores a fuller string body and firmer bass support while preserving the long-breathed melodic character; the join enlarges the sound without turning the line into rapid passagework. Ornament has connected the solo voice to the surrounding song. As the ensemble gathers, listen for its sustained melody carrying the expansion rather than the number of attacks supplying all the force.
transitions.evidence: The Renewed orchestral song boundary is 5:42, a novelty peak. Relative level rises through 5:45–6:05 while attack density decreases. The score supplies the fuller G-major lyrical writing; the report does not establish an exact hand-over between solo violin and string section.

transitions.title: The song leaves a lighter codetta
transitions.how: The final expansion releases its weight without abandoning G major. Wind decoration and lighter string articulation replace the full sustained statement; the bass continues to support closure while fragments of the melodic material become more exposed. The movement ends by reducing the scale of its gestures, not by importing the finale’s force. G-major harmony can remain settled while the orchestration changes from a collective song to small, separated responses.
transitions.evidence: The Quiet close boundary is 7:30; relative level and brightness fall across 7:25–7:40. The written codetta supplies the lighter wind-and-string texture and G-major close, also discussed by Serotsky at http://musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm. The timestamp does not claim a final cadence or last attack.

facts: Naval College in Saint Petersburg; composition with Mily Balakirev, followed by intensive private study
Saint Petersburg Conservatory from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Married the pianist and composer Nadezhda Purgold in 1872; she assisted with arrangements and editorial work
Fifteen operas, three symphonies, orchestral suites and overtures, songs and teaching books
composer.background:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in Tikhvin into a family with a tradition of naval service. He entered the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, while continuing piano lessons and attending opera. His teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Balakirev in 1861. The young officer began a symphony before he had the theoretical equipment expected of a conservatory composition student. A naval voyage on the clipper Almaz took him abroad in 1862–65, interrupting regular contact with the circle while work on the symphony continued. Balakirev conducted the First Symphony in Saint Petersburg in 1865.

His early colleagues included Mussorgsky, Borodin and Cui. With Balakirev they became the group known as the Five, united by friendship and cultural argument despite their differing methods. Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral picture Sadko, first written in 1867, already connects a supernatural subject with an unusual pitch organisation. The sea musician’s underwater world encouraged scales and chord relationships outside ordinary major and minor. His experience of ships and oceans gave the subject a biographical setting.
composer.epithet: A naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of Russian fairy-tale opera.
